Quality Coffee Systems · Walkthrough

From a blank quote to a sent email

The whole flow, start to finish, on the real system with real machines from the catalogue. Ten steps, about two minutes of work once you have done it once.

Recorded 12 August 2026 · the email in step 9 was genuinely sent

The whole thing, in about forty seconds

Worth watching once before reading the steps — it's easier to follow the detail when you know where it's going.

1

Open the Quote builder

It lives in ERP Core — the document icon down the left rail. You land on an empty quote with the standard QCS terms already written in: warranty, water softener, freight, payment terms, the ordering process. Those come out on every quote, so nobody has to remember them.

2

Say who it's for

To is the company. Start typing and it suggests customers already on file — pick the suggestion rather than typing it out, because that is what links the quote to their record. Get it wrong and the quote still prints fine, it just won't show up on their history or in the pipeline. Attn is the person, and Re / subject is what this is about; both appear at the top of the quote.

3

Add the machines

Type into Add from catalogue and pick the machine. Price, dealer discount and the description come across on their own, and the preview on the right updates as you go. Quantity, price and discount are all editable on the line if this deal is different. The % button beside a discount switches it to $ if you'd rather take a flat amount off.

4

Check the numbers

Everything adds up live: list price, discounts, delivery and install, net price. Delivery is $500 by default — tick Included when you're absorbing it and the quote says “Included” instead of a figure. If the quote looks right here, it will look right to the customer.

5

Save it

Save quote gives it a number (Q-YYYYMM-NNNN) and — this is the part worth knowing — creates an opportunity in the Pipeline for that customer. That's how a quote turns into something the business can see and follow up on, rather than a PDF in someone's downloads folder.

6

Find it under Saved quotes

Every saved quote is here with its number, customer, subject, value and status. From this row you can re-open it to edit, email it, mark it sent by hand, or record that the customer accepted or declined — which moves the deal along the pipeline for you.

7

Press Email…

The address is filled in from the customer's record. Add a Cc if someone else should see it. The two tick boxes are worth understanding: Attach spec sheets pulls the datasheets held against those machines in the catalogue, and Show product photos beside each line puts the machine's picture next to its row in the email. Underneath, Choose Files is for anything else — an install sheet, a site photo, a floor plan.

8

Write a line, then send

The message sits above the quote, in your voice. It's optional, but a quote that opens with “thanks for the site visit yesterday” reads like a person sent it. Then Send quote — it goes from info@qualitycoffeesystems.ca, not from your own mailbox.

9

Read what it tells you

It reports back exactly what went: who it reached, which files attached, how many photos are in the quote, and anything sent as a link instead of an attachment. That last one is normal — spec sheets can be several megabytes each, and past a certain size the email would be rejected, so the biggest ones become links. The customer gets them either way.

10

It's marked sent, and logged

The quote flips to SENT, the deal moves to Quote Sent in the pipeline, and the send is written onto the customer's history with the date and who it went to. Nobody has to remember to update anything. When the customer replies, come back to this row and press Accepted or Declined.

A few things worth knowing

Picking the customer from the suggestions matters. It is the only thing linking the quote to their record. Type the name freehand and the quote works, but it won't appear on their history, and it won't create the opportunity in the pipeline.

Send one to yourself first. Put your own address in the To box on a real quote and read it as if you were the customer. If a sentence sounds off or the layout looks cheap, tell us — much easier to change now than after it has gone to fifty people.

Spec sheets sometimes arrive as links. Some datasheets are several megabytes; past a certain total the email would be rejected outright, so the largest become links in the body instead. The confirmation always tells you which ones. Nothing is silently dropped.

Mark the outcome when you hear back. Accepted or Declined on the saved-quote row is what keeps the pipeline honest — without it, a won deal sits in "Quote Sent" forever.
